newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Earth summit to end with many goals unfulfilled.
newsitem.headline: Earth summit to end with many goals unfulfilled.

text.p: The U.N. Earth Summit drew towards a close on Friday and its chairman said the world had failed to achieve many of the ambitious goals for protecting the planet set five years ago in Rio de Janeiro.

"Lets call a spade a spade. Over five years, not enough has been done," said U.N. General Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia, chairman of the week-long gathering of more than 170 nations called to review progress since the landmark 1992 Rio environmental conference.
Razali described the failure to live up to the promise of Rio as an "absence of political will."
As if to confirm this, delegates said the final summit document would not, as planned, include a political statement of intent because governments could not agree on one.

Another issue that remained unsettled was commitments by industrial states, accounting for half the world's pollution, to lower greenhouse gas emissions as they prepare for a climate conference in Kyoto, Japan in December.
The European Union wanted definite goals now, which the United States, Japan, Canada and Australia rejected.
But Washington agreed to "realistic and legally binding" targets by Kyoto that would "significantly" reduce the greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
Japan, however, objected and last-minute language was still being sought.
Razali said the meeting would end on Friday night without drifting into the weekend as some delegates had feared.

He said the bleak outcome of this meeting should go down as "a very honest attempt" without papering over differences. "I'm very happy we didn't go for the gloss. We went for the real thing, an honest appraisal," he said.

Razali said he took heart from language in the final declaration calling for phasing out leaded gasoline and agreements to expand government talks on supplying fresh water and sanitation to the world's poor.
Barbara Bramble of the World Wildlife Fund also spoke of progress in "slow bits." But she said: "There is a disconnect in time between what is being done and what is needed."

Missing from the final document are firm commitments by rich countries to assist developing nations, particularly those left out of corporate financial investments. This issue has prevented the Third World from agreeing to ecological programmes the industrial nations want.
"Since 1992 a sense of parochialism has has spread over much of the developed world (that) has affected the willingness of countries to make available funds or technological transfers," Razali said.

Bramble, an expert on finances, said she expected American proposals in Kyoto to fail unless some progress was made on foreign aid. The United States is expected to call for a lowering of emissions in developing countries like China, the world's second largest polluter, as well as in rich states.
Cliff Curtis of Greenpeace International, however, complimented President Bill Clinton for emphasising climate change in his Thursday night speech to the summit.
"Throughout this week it (climate change) has gotten a critical amount of attention, consciousness-raising," he said.
Environmental groups were pleased with the results of the meeting on strategy to protect the world's dwindling forests.
Canada and the European Union lost out on their proposal to start negotiations immediately on a binding treaty that would introduce standards for the logging trade.
Instead the issue will be considered again in 2000. The United States, Brazil and India as well as most ecologists opposed a treaty, preferring to see existing agreements enforced.
